analysis.one_liner: Raises federal penalties on insurers and health plans that violate surprise-medical-billing protections.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2025 with 38 cosponsors split evenly between parties, but was only referred to three House committees and has seen no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2022 No Surprises Act already bans most surprise medical bills from out-of-network providers at in-network hospitals, but enforcement against insurers and plans that break the rules has been light. This bill raises the civil penalty from $100 per day to $10,000 per violation for the core balance billing rules, creates a new penalty worth triple the unpaid amount plus interest for plans or providers that pay late or not at all after an arbitration decision, and requires the government to report to Congress twice a year on audits, complaints, and enforcement actions.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with employer-sponsored or individual insurance gain stronger protection against plans and insurers that violate the federal rules against surprise balance billing, since violations would carry penalties of $10,000 per failure rather than $100 per day. Patients also benefit indirectly from rules that force prompt payment after arbitration decisions, and Congress and the public gain visibility through semiannual reports on audits, complaints, and penalties.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the penalty for plans and insurers that violate balance billing protections to $10,000 per failure, instead of the current $100 per day.
Adds a penalty worth three times the payment gap, plus interest, on any plan, insurer, or out-of-network provider that pays late or not at all after an independent dispute resolution decision.

Requires the federal government to report to Congress twice a year on audits, consumer and provider complaints, enforcement actions, and the dollar value of penalties issued under the No Surprises Act.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employer group health plans bear the higher penalties for noncompliance, and out-of-network providers or facilities that pay late after an arbitration decision would owe triple the unpaid difference plus interest. Some of the compliance cost could ultimately show up in premiums.

drawbacks.text: The bill also imposes new payment-timing and triple-damages rules on out-of-network providers and facilities, not just insurers, so some providers who lose dispute decisions and pay slowly would face the same steep penalties.
Stronger penalties only matter if federal agencies actually enforce them; the bill adds reporting on enforcement, but it does not itself mandate more audits or complaint investigations.
Heavier penalties on health plans could eventually be passed through to employers and premiums, though the bill targets violations that are already illegal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but modest: stronger fines and a triple-damages rule give regulators and consumers real leverage against plans and insurers that ignore the No Surprises Act, and semiannual public reporting would expose which plans keep violating the rules. The costs fall mainly on plans and providers that already owe money under the law, which is the point of a penalty. The main weakness is that penalties alone do not fix slow federal enforcement, and the added payment rules apply to both sides, so providers who drag out disputes face the same triple-damages exposure. Overall it is a reasonably targeted enforcement bill, though one that sits in three committees and may go nowhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to three House committees in July 2025, and no committee has taken it up since.

narrative.text: H.R. 4710, the No Surprises Act Enforcement Act, was introduced in the House on July 23, 2025 by Rep. Gregory Murphy.
It attracted 38 cosponsors, 21 Republicans and 17 Democrats, showing two-party interest in stronger enforcement of surprise billing protections.
The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Workforce committees, and no further action has been taken.
The complete action history shows only the introduction and committee referrals, with no hearings, markups, or floor votes.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet; insurers and health plans benefit from the continued lack of stronger penalties while it sits in committee.

for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan support in the House.

sides.party_line_note: The 38 cosponsors split 21 Republicans and 17 Democrats, so support is genuinely bipartisan, though no committee has acted.

industries.industry: Health insurers and employer group health plans
industries.note: The bill raises penalties to $10,000 per violation for plans and insurers that break balance billing rules, and adds triple-damages penalties for slow or missing payments after arbitration. Stronger enforcement protects patients from surprise bills, so the industry's interest here runs against the public's.

industries.industry: Out-of-network doctors, hospitals, and air ambulance operators
industries.note: These providers are the usual winners when plans ignore or delay No Surprises Act payments; the bill gives them a triple-damages remedy for unpaid awards, but also makes them pay penalties and interest if they are the party paying late.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to three committees simultaneously often go nowhere, and this one has had no action since July 2025. Unless the relevant committees schedule a hearing or markup, it is likely to die quietly at the end of the Congress, as most bills without committee action do.
